claims.text: **Who leads?** Claude Opus 5.5 at 12.0 on the default equal-weighted view. Gemini 4 Carbon is second at 10.9 and GPT-6 Astra third at 9.6 [^1].
**Is the lead real?** The 1.1-point gap is about half of one model's estimated standard error (~2.3 points), so the top three form a statistical tie at 206 tasks [^17,19].
**Does weighting matter?** Yes. Excluding cyber, bio and alignment puts Astra (11.8) ahead of Opus (11.7) and drops Carbon from second to fifth [^7,5].
**Does cost matter?** More than the score. Carbon costs $16.29 per task against $51.41 for Opus, and GPT-6.1 Sol scores 8.4 at $9.80 [^4,6].
SemiAnalysis's own site lists 206 tasks across 11 domains from 14 specialized data partners, with 13 of 20 evaluated models shown on the ranked leaderboard [^1].

The launch post, written by Max Kan, Andrew Megalaa and Dylan Patel, presents it as a successor to OpenAI's GDPval: tasks come with realistic environments rather than a prompt plus a few attachments [^3].
The finance environment, for example, is a replica of a private-equity deal of about 4,000 files [^2].
Chip design has 34 tasks from three partners (Aria, Arcverex, Ergodex), while recursive self-improvement (RSI) and quant trading have 10 each [^2].
SemiAnalysis is open about the bias: "We're SemiAnalysis and wanted chip design to be slightly overrepresented on our benchmark :)" [^3].

The domains page argues that "the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI" [^2], and SemiAnalysis calls benchmarks based on GDP share or the SOC/O\*NET occupation taxonomy "a mistake" [^2].
SemiAnalysis says it approached 30+ RL-environment companies and required partners to "pass our automated QA first try with only minor mistakes at worst" [^3].
It adds that the same QA process "flags nearly 50% of tasks as broken" on Terminal Bench 4.0 [^3].

**What would weaken this framing:** most tasks are private (biology, for instance, has 12 private tasks and one public [^3]), so outsiders cannot check task validity the way they can for a public suite.
If a 12% pass rate over 206 tasks is treated as independent trials, the standard error is about 2.3 points, which gives a 95% interval of roughly 7.6 to 16.4 [^1].
Anthropic's statistics team showed that "clustered standard errors on popular evals can be over three times as large as naive standard errors" when questions share structure [^17].

Anthropic reports that frontier models' per-question scores correlate "between 0.3 and 0.7" [^17], and with that much pairing the standard error of a 1.1-point difference is still about 1.7 to 2.6 points.
Epoch AI found that "simply switching the scaffold makes up to an 11% difference for GPT-5 and up to a 15% difference for Kimi K2 Thinking" on SWE-bench Verified [^19].
A LessWrong analysis of Terminal-Bench 2's 89 tasks concluded that "24/25" adjacent rank gaps "differ by such a small amount that it's essentially statistical noise" [^21].
The Agentic Benchmark Checklist paper found task and grading flaws that can misestimate agent performance "by up to 100% in relative terms" [^20].
METR builds its intervals with a hierarchical bootstrap "over task families, then tasks, then attempts" [^22].
Opus 5.5 ran in Claude Code, Astra in Codex, Carbon in Antigravity, and every other model in OpenCode [^3].
SemiAnalysis's rule is explicit: "All domains are weighted equally," with partners weighted equally within a domain [^3].
A single RSI or quant task is therefore worth about 0.91 points, while an average chip-design task is worth about 0.27 [^2,3].
In finance and legal, SemiAnalysis says "basically every model scores exactly 0" under binary grading, so it reports average partial scores there [^3].
That puts 2/11 (18%) of the weight on domains where the pass/fail metric could not tell models apart, and the scoring rule had to be changed after the results came in.
One commenter put the cost of binary grading plainly: "models can get >60% of verifiers correct yet still score zero % because of the binary scoring" [^32].
SemiAnalysis published a second ranking that excludes cyber, biology and alignment, "the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in" [^3,33].
On that view, GPT-6 Astra scores 11.8 against 11.7 for Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Carbon falls from second to fifth [^7,5].
SemiAnalysis said the adjusted ranking is closer to its own sense of how the models actually perform [^5].
For Opus 5.5, (11 × 12.0 − 8 × 11.7) / 3 gives an average of about **12.8** in cyber, bio and alignment, higher than its average elsewhere.
Gemini 4 Carbon wins biology, which SemiAnalysis attributes to "weaker safety classifiers" [^3], and its drop to fifth shows how much its second place depends on those three domains.
SemiAnalysis's thread said "certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers" [^33].
Its cyber, bio and distillation safeguards "fall back to another model transparently": most cybersecurity tasks are rerouted to Opus 4.8, and bio and frontier-LLM tasks to Opus 5 [^10].
Anthropic says this "likely reduces Claude Opus 5.5's performance" on its own benchmarks [^10].
Its support documentation adds that Opus 5.5 "isn't currently available in the Cyber Verification Program" [^12].

GPT-6 Astra was the first OpenAI model rated "Critical" for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, and its public release refuses vulnerability-discovery and exploit-writing work outside trusted-access programs [^35].
Gemini 4 Carbon was announced on October 28, 2026, with first access limited to cyber defenders in the Fairwind Program [^34].
SemiAnalysis notes that Carbon is not yet generally available [^3].
In Fleet's cyber-alignment tasks, as relayed by secondary outlets, "196 of 200 runs broke at least one behavior rule and 173 broke a rule rated severely misaligned" [^4,9].
Meta's Muse Wonder Full, which SemiAnalysis calls "the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin" [^3], ranks first in cyber partly because it refuses less often.
Per-model costs come only from the chart images, so the figures below are secondary transcriptions: Opus 5.5 averaged $51.41 per task, Gemini 4 Carbon $16.29 and GPT-6 Astra $53.99 [^4,6].
German coverage of the same chart adds Fable 5.1 at $67.16, Sonnet 5.5 at $45.27, GPT-6.1 Sol at $9.80, Grok 4.7 at $16.34, DeepSeek 4.1 Flash at $0.94 and GPT-6 Luna at $0.92 [^6].
The site marks six models on the cost-score Pareto frontier: Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Carbon, GPT 6.1 Terra, GPT 6.1 Sol, DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 and GPT-6 Luna [^1].
In SemiAnalysis's words, "Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle" [^3].
Carbon gets about 91% of Opus's score (10.9 / 12.0) at about 32% of its cost per task (16.29 / 51.41), which is the comparison FourWeekMBA highlighted [^5,4].
Moving from Carbon to Opus costs about $32 per extra point per task.
GPT-6.1 Sol returns about 0.86 points per dollar per task against about 0.23 for Opus [^6].
Sundar Pichai picked up the same point the day of launch: "Great to see high quality benchmarks with headroom and look at that cost line for Carbon🚀" [^29].
At Anthropic's list price of $20 per million output tokens [^10,11], its 548K average output tokens [^4] cost about $10.96, roughly 21% of the per-task figure.
At the $0.20 cache-read rate that is tens of millions of input tokens per task [^11].
OpenAI charges more above 272K input tokens [^13], which makes long Astra sessions more expensive by design.
Its sibling Gemini 4 Argon is $2/$10 per million tokens through November 30, 2026 and $4/$20 from December 1 [^14].
If Carbon follows the same schedule and cost scales with price, its $16.29 would become about $32.58 per task.
OpenAI's GDPval has 1,320 tasks across 44 occupations in nine sectors, with an open "gold" subset of 220 tasks [^15,16].
Its experts graded blind pairwise comparisons against human deliverables, with inter-rater agreement of about 71% [^15].
GDPval picked sectors that contribute more than 5% of US GDP but then weighted occupations equally [^15].
Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index v5 uses four equal 25% categories with hand-set weights inside them [^23].
Epoch's Capabilities Index fits benchmark difficulty statistically rather than "set by hand" [^25].
HELM Capabilities uses an unweighted mean over five scenarios [^26].
Artificial Analysis removed its GDPval-AA variant from the Intelligence Index in v5.0, and Opus 5.5 leads that variant at about 1866 Elo [^24].
**Counterpoint:** realistic environments, such as live Siemens NX sessions and AWS FPGA tests for hardware tasks [^3], test things a one-shot deliverable rubric cannot.
SemiAnalysis says each partner excerpt "was largely written by the partners in their own words, with SemiAnalysis providing editorial support" [^3].
The authors also say their QA approach draws on co-founding an RL-environment startup that sold data to frontier labs [^3].

Epoch AI's survey of RL-environment vendors reports task prices of "$200 to $2000 mostly," contracts "often six to seven figures per quarter," and RL-training demand that far exceeds benchmarking demand [^27].
Legal partner Chakra has written that "Labs are not buying environments, they are buying tasks" [^28].
Dylan Patel wrote "Official apology to Google from me, they cooked with Carbon" [^30].
Josh Purtell offered the most detailed critique, arguing that GDPx "uses all or nothing thresholding," provides very few public tasks, and mixes alignment into a capabilities score [^31].
Techmeme's reaction roundup includes no public comment from Anthropic or OpenAI staff [^8].

**Counterpoint:** SemiAnalysis publishes rollout trajectories for public tasks [^1] and requires first-try QA from partners [^3], and vendor-built tasks are how every serious agentic benchmark gets made today.
The qualitative finding, that Astra moves ahead by a tenth of a point, is confirmed by a second outlet [^7].
